newsitem.title: UK: Britain unveils plans to bring in new millennium.
newsitem.headline: Britain unveils plans to bring in new millennium.

text.p: Britain unveiled plans on Thursday for a 750-million-pound ($1.2-billion) exhibition to mark the new millennium, promising it will be the most "thought-provoking experience on the planet in the year 2000."

The controversial project, which was given the go-ahead last week by Prime Minister Tony Blair after a wave of adverse publicity over cost and content, will centre around a huge steel dome to be built at Greenwich on the bank of the Thames.
"Greenwich is the home of time," Minister Without Portfolio Peter Mandelson told a news conference.
"The meridian line runs through the exhibition site. That is why the rest of the world will be looking to Britain - the new millennium will, literally, start here.
"It is a chance for Britain to make a big statement about itself and to the rest of the world."
Stressing that it will be much more than an exhibition, Mandelson, who will be in charge of the overall project, re-christened it the Millennium Experience.
The Greenwich dome, designed by Lord Richard Rogers, the architect of France's Pompidou Centre, will be the focus of the celebrations.
But National Heritage Secretary Chris Smith said the dawn of the new millennium will be marked throughout Britain with projects and exhibits which will create tens of thousands of jobs.
"It is important to put it in context; it (the Millennium Experience) represents only a quarter of the Millennium Commission's overall commitment of more than 1.6 billion pounds," he said.
Before approving the dome project, which was the brainchild of former Conservative deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine, Blair set out several conditions it must meet.

It must leave a lasting legacy for future generations, it much be cost-efficient, it must have an interesting, exciting concept that will involve the entire country, and there has to be a management shake-up of the project.
Mandelson said his team took seriously various criticisms of the exhibition's size, cost and content but it needed to be big to accommodate millions of people who will pass through it in 2000.
The government had decided to go ahead with the project because millions of pounds of public investment would have been wasted it they had called it off.
The Millennium Commission, using funds from the National Lottery, will provide 450 million pounds for the project.
Another 135 million pounds is expected from ticket sales while sponsorship from private industry is expected to make up much of the shortfall.
"I believe that once business sees who else is getting involved no one will want to be left out," Mandelson predicted.
Before they toppled the long-ruling Conservatives in the May 1 election, the Labour Party had been cool to the project and the top-selling Sun newspaper ran a campaign to dump the scheme.
But Mandelson said it was now all systems go and the aim was to bring cultural enrichment that will last long after the millennium year has ended.

Time will be the theme of the Millennium Experience which will give visitors a glimpse of what the future will hold in terms of lifestyle, health, work, and how the environment, housing, energy and transport will change.
Theatre impressario Cameron Mackintosh, whose plays include Les Miserables, Cats and Oliver, will also produce a multi-media and live performance show for the exhibition. ($ = 0.600 British Pounds)
